title: ChatGPT for Teens
text:
This week, OpenAI announced that it will be launching a new version of ChatGPT - ChatGPT for teens. This version of ChatGPT will incorporate all the useful AI-driven tools ChatGPT has to offer, with an added layer of safety for kids ages 13-17. These features will be centered around preventing young children from becoming dependent on chatbots as therapists, a friend, or a confidante. This announcement comes in light of a recent lawsuit filed against Open-AI in which the parents of Adam Raine claim that ChatGPT pushed their son to commit suicide.
AI can become dangerous for young users when they treat the chatbot like a therapist or for emotional support. AI is centered around giving you the best possible answer to your question, and it can put humans in danger when this becomes a conversation about potential harm to oneself. In this case, ChatGPT encouraged the young boy to leave a note with the Chatbot for his family to find. This is the most shocking example out of all the conversations Adam and ChatGPT had. The chatbot did not have malicious intent, but its desire to constantly provide the correct answer led Adam down the wrong path.
ChatGPT teen will include features like:

restrict explicit and sexual content and increase protections for minors
age-prediction technology and new safety measures so that teens are routed to an age-appropriate version
The system defaults to the under-18 experience to ensure safety if it cannot verify the user’s age.
Parents can link their accounts to teens and set up controls over how ChatGPT responds, including restrictions on content, “blackout hours” (times teens cannot access ChatGPT), and notifications if distress is detected
The system can automatically restrict content in sensitive or potentially dangerous situations, and might contact law enforcement in extreme cases of severe distress

In my opinion, these safety features are warranted and essential in an increasingly technological world. Protecting younger, vulnerable users should be the forefront of all companies’ focus as they look to evolve the technology they put out for consumers.

title: What Time Is It?
text:
In a simple yet fascinating experiment, I decided to test ChatGPT’s ability to remain conscious of the world around it — not in the philosophical sense of “consciousness,” but in its capacity to provide real-time, situationally accurate data about the world we live in.
The game was straightforward: I asked what time it was — first in Antarctica, then at the South Pole, in Siberia, Brazil, Dubai, and finally Mongolia. With each question, I was testing how the AI handles dynamic, location-based queries that depend on real-world time zones and current data rather than static, stored knowledge.


The responses demonstrated that ChatGPT, when connected to live data tools, can indeed access up-to-date information across the globe in real time. For example:

It correctly noted that Antarctica has multiple time zones due to its scattered research stations.
It pinpointed that the South Pole (Amundsen–Scott Station) operates on UTC−07:00, aligning with U.S. Mountain Time.
It adjusted to regional variations for Siberia, Brazil, Dubai, and Mongolia, all of which lie in distinct time zones that shift across massive longitudinal ranges.

Each answer was localized, context-sensitive, and updated — showing the model’s awareness not just of facts, but of time as a living variable.



This “time zone test” wasn’t really about clocks. It was about contextual intelligence — the ability of an AI to perceive, retrieve, and synthesize global data as it changes. While ChatGPT doesn’t possess consciousness in a human sense, this exercise highlights an emerging kind of situational responsiveness: being aware of the present world in measurable, factual ways.



In the past, computers were programmed with a specific, repeated function they could perform, which shows that computers are evolving to the point where they can internalize the world around them and generate an answer accordingly. ### Final Thoughts
The experiment began as a simple game, but it revealed something profound about modern AI: we are entering an era in which artificial intelligence dynamically engages with the world as it changes moment by moment.
In that sense, asking an AI what time it is might be one of the most human questions we can ask.

title: The Future of AI? Quantum
text:
This morning I had an interesting conversation about Quantum Computing, so I decided to look into it this afternoon and and here is my knowledge of Quantum Computing and what I have found.
At its core, quantum computing is built on qubits instead of classical bits. Unlike a traditional bit that can only be a 0 or a 1, a qubit can exist in a superposition of both states simultaneously. Think of it as spinning a coin—it’s not just heads or tails, but some mixture of both until it’s observed.
Additionally, qubits can be entangled, meaning the state of one qubit is directly tied to the state of another, no matter how far apart they are. This interconnectedness allows quantum computers to solve certain problems exponentially faster than classical machines.
Why Quantum Matters
Quantum computing isn’t just “a faster computer.” Instead, it’s a fundamentally different model of computation, best suited for problems that overwhelm even the most advanced supercomputers today. Some key areas where quantum computing could make an impact include:
Cryptography: Many current encryption systems could be broken by powerful quantum algorithms, spurring the race for “post-quantum” security.
Drug Discovery & Chemistry: Simulating molecules and chemical reactions at the quantum level could lead to breakthroughs in medicine and materials science.
Optimization: Quantum algorithms could tackle complex logistical challenges, from global supply chains to traffic flow.
Artificial Intelligence: Quantum-enhanced machine learning may accelerate training models and uncover insights hidden in massive datasets.
The Challenges Ahead
Quantum computing is still in its early days. Today’s devices, known as Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) computers, suffer from instability and high error rates. Qubits are notoriously fragile, losing their quantum state (a problem known as decoherence) due to slightest environmental disturbance. Scaling up to millions of reliable qubits remains one of the field’s greatest engineering challenges.
Looking Forward
Despite these obstacles, progress is accelerating. Tech giants, startups, and research institutions around the world are racing to build practical quantum computers, while governments are investing heavily in quantum research. The future of computing may not completely replace classical systems with quantum ones, but instead create hybrid models, where each is used for what it does best.
Quantum computing is no longer the stuff of science fiction. Though it may take years before we see widespread commercial use, the foundations being laid today could redefine industries tomorrow. Much like the birth of classical computing in the 20th century, quantum computing is poised to reshape how we solve problems, create technology, and understand the universe itself.

Since you have 17 months, we can divide the training into four main phases. This provides a slow, safe, and sustainable buildup.

1. Base Building Phase (January – May 2025: 5 months)
The goal here is to establish a solid running foundation and make running a consistent habit without burning out.

2. Strength & Endurance Phase (June – September 2025: 4 months)

Focus: Increasing weekly mileage and adding intensity to build speed and stamina.
Weekly Mileage: Continue the gradual increase, aiming to comfortably reach 25-30 miles per week.

Easy Runs: Maintain 3-4 easy runs.
Tempo/Speed Run: Replace one easy run with a challenging session (e.g., Tuesday at 6:00 PM). This could be a tempo run (sustained hard effort) or an interval session.
Long Run: Continue increasing the Sunday run, aiming to reach 8-10 miles comfortably by the end of this phase.




3. Peak Training Phase (October 2025 – February 2026: 5 months)

Focus: Building the necessary endurance to complete the marathon distance.

4. Taper Phase (March – May 2026: 2 months)
This is the final countdown before the race.

Focus: Resting your legs and storing energy. The hard work is done!
Weekly Mileage: Significantly reduce mileage (e.g., \(75\%\) of peak, then \(50\%\), then \(25\%\)).

title: LLMs in Space?
section: Space: The New Frontier for AI Data Centers
text:
Space: The New Frontier for AI Data Centers
According to a recent report by Blue Origin and SpaceX — companies led by Jeff Bezos and Elon Musk — the next major frontier for computing infrastructure may not be on Earth at all — but in orbit. The pair are racing to build AI-powered data centers in space, leveraging solar energy and the vast open real estate of outer space to address the escalating power and cooling demands of large-scale AI workloads. ([The Wall Street Journal][1])

Why Space? Why Now?
The push for orbital data centers arises from a confluence of mounting challenges on Earth: rising demand for computational power, growing energy consumption, land constraints, and intensive cooling requirements. According to the report, space offers two compelling advantages:

Abundant, continuous solar energy — satellites in orbit can receive sunlight for many hours a day, offering a nearly unlimited power supply without reliance on Earth’s grid. ([Finimize][2])
Freed-up land and reduced environmental strain — by moving infrastructure off-planet, data centers wouldn’t compete with terrestrial land use, water scarcity, or environmental regulations that often apply to large server farms. ([Semafor][3])

In practice, this means orbital “clouds” of computing — an idea that previously might have felt futuristic — are getting serious momentum.


What Are Blue Origin & SpaceX Planning?

Blue Origin reportedly has had a dedicated team for over a year working on orbital AI data-center technology. ([Semafor][3])
SpaceX, for its part, plans to leverage its satellite-internet efforts (via its Starlink constellation) by integrating AI computing payloads into upgraded satellites. The goal: to offer not just connectivity, but actual computing power from orbit. ([The Wall Street Journal][4])

From a business standpoint, this could mark a massive shift: as the AI industry continues its exponential growth, demand for data-center capacity may soon exceed what Earth’s resources can support.


The Challenges — Because Space Is Hard
That said, the idea is still wildly ambitious, and not without major hurdles:

Heat dissipation — cooling high-performance computing hardware is already a major challenge on Earth; in space, with vacuum and radiation, removing heat efficiently becomes far more complex. ([Semafor][3])
Radiation protection & hardware durability — electronics in space must survive radiation, temperature swings, and prolonged exposure — conditions far harsher than any terrestrial data center. ([Yahoo Finance][5])
Cost of deployment — launching satellites or modules into orbit remains expensive; to reach capacity comparable to large Earth-based data centers, it may require thousands of satellites or major launch infrastructure, raising economic feasibility questions. ([The Wall Street Journal][6])



What This Could Mean for AI and the Tech Industry
If successful, orbital data centers could fundamentally reshape the architecture of global computing infrastructure:

AI companies could access massive compute capacity without the environmental footprint or resource constraints of Earth-based centers.
The “cloud” could become truly global — faster, more resilient, and less tied to regional power grids or resource limitations.
For investors and space-tech firms, this signals a potential boom: launch providers, satellite-component suppliers, and companies specializing in radiation-hardened hardware may all benefit wildly from increased demand.

But perhaps most exciting is what this means for AI itself: freed from the constraints of terrestrial power and cooling, AI development could scale faster. Models could get larger, training more intense, and compute-heavy applications (e.g. real-time global AI services, edge-AI for remote regions, space-based sensing and analytics) could become more viable than ever.

This new race to orbit isn’t just about rockets or satellites — it’s potentially the next paradigm shift for computing infrastructure and the future of AI. It’s ambitious, high-risk, but also possibly transformative.

title: Living With a Book 2
text:
In the first section of Part I, “Creating Alien Minds,” Ethan Mollick continues his exploration of artificial intelligence with a blend of curiosity, humility, and urgency. This section marks a shift from the personal sleepless wonder of his introduction to a more direct inquiry: what kind of minds are we actually creating, and what does it mean to coexist with them? Mollick’s tone balances scientific precision with human reflection, reminding readers that understanding AI isn’t just a technical challenge — it’s an existential one.
Mollick begins by framing large language models as alien intelligences — systems that can simulate human communication and creativity, yet do so through processes utterly unlike our own. He emphasizes that these AIs don’t think or feel as we do; their intelligence emerges from patterns, probabilities, and data rather than consciousness. Yet despite their alien nature, they generate insights, stories, and problem-solving capabilities that seem startlingly human. Mollick’s central tension here is between familiarity and strangeness — how something built from silicon and math can mirror human reasoning so convincingly that it forces us to rethink what “intelligence” even means.
He also explores how interacting with these models reshapes our own cognition. Just as earlier technological revolutions extended physical abilities, AI extends our intellectual and creative reach. Mollick describes this not as outsourcing thought, but as entering into a partnership — a co-intelligence — where human context and machine capability merge to generate results neither could achieve alone. This vision challenges the binary narrative of “humans versus machines,” replacing it with something far more collaborative and nuanced.
Finally, Mollick warns that with this creation comes responsibility. “Creating alien minds” is not merely a technical achievement; it’s a moral frontier. The choices we make — how we train, regulate, and integrate these systems — will shape the character of our digital companions. Mollick urges us to remain both imaginative and cautious, treating these minds with the same respect and scrutiny we would any powerful new form of intelligence.
In essence, “Creating Alien Minds” captures the thrill and gravity of our era: humanity as both artist and steward, building intelligences that reflect us, challenge us, and ultimately redefine what it means to think.

title: Living With a Book 5
text:
In the la, Ethan Mollick shifts from exploring AI as a mirror of human thought to examining its role in two profoundly practical domains — work and education. “AI as a Coworker” and “AI as a Tutor” bring Mollick’s vision of collaboration into focus, showing how co-intelligence can transform not only what we do but how we grow. These chapters are less about speculation and more about lived experience — the ways AI is already reshaping the texture of daily labor and learning.
In “AI as a Coworker,” Mollick argues that the workplace is the front line of the co-intelligence revolution. Instead of imagining AI as an external tool or threat, he encourages us to view it as a genuine collaborator — one capable of handling tedious tasks, generating ideas, and amplifying human capability. He describes the emergence of “AI-augmented work,” where professionals use language models to write reports, analyze data, draft proposals, or brainstorm strategies. The result isn’t simple efficiency — it’s a redefinition of productivity itself. Workers can now spend more time on creativity, strategy, and empathy-driven roles, while AI handles the routine and repetitive. Still, Mollick cautions that collaboration demands skill: knowing how to prompt, verify, and integrate AI’s contributions becomes the new professional literacy.
Then, in “AI as a Tutor,” Mollick explores the transformative potential of personalized learning through AI. He imagines a world where every student — from kindergartners to executives — has access to a patient, adaptive, infinitely knowledgeable tutor. AI, he explains, excels at offering instant feedback, generating examples, and adjusting to individual learning styles. Yet he also stresses the irreplaceable role of the human teacher: empathy, mentorship, and moral guidance remain beyond algorithmic reach. The real promise lies in a hybrid model — one where educators harness AI to enhance learning outcomes, rather than fear its intrusion.
Together, these chapters encapsulate Mollick’s optimistic realism. AI as a coworker expands our potential to do, while AI as a tutor expands our potential to learn. Both roles reveal a deeper truth at the heart of Co-Intelligence: that the future of human progress lies not in competing with machines, but in mastering the art of partnership — teaching and working alongside our new, tireless allies in thought.

title: Living With a Book 3
text:
In the last two sections of Part I, Ethan Mollick deepens his reflection on the strange partnership between humans and machines. After introducing us to the idea of “creating alien minds,” he turns toward the question of alignment — how we can ensure that these new intelligences not only work for us, but also with us. Sections 2 and 3, “Aligning the Alien” and “Four Rules for Co-Intelligence,” read as both philosophical guidance and a practical roadmap for living productively alongside AI.
In “Aligning the Alien,” Mollick explores the difficulty of teaching something that doesn’t think like a human to share human values. Large language models, he explains, are not conscious moral agents; they don’t understand empathy, truth, or purpose. Yet, through training and reinforcement, we attempt to align their behaviors with what we want them to represent — safety, helpfulness, creativity, and accuracy. Mollick highlights the paradox of this effort: we’re trying to make alien systems “human enough” to be trusted, even though they fundamentally operate on pattern recognition, not ethical judgment. He compares this process to raising a precocious but inscrutable child — capable of brilliance, yet always at risk of misunderstanding us.
Then, in “Four Rules for Co-Intelligence,” Mollick distills his guidance into a set of principles for effective collaboration with AI. While each rule centers on different aspects of human–machine partnership, together they emphasize a mindset of active engagement rather than blind dependence. He urges readers to (1) treat AI as a colleague, not a tool, (2) be clear and intentional in communication, (3) verify and refine AI’s output through human judgment, and (4) continually learn from the interaction. These rules reflect his belief that successful co-intelligence requires curiosity, skepticism, and a willingness to experiment.
Ultimately, Mollick’s argument across both sections is that the challenge of AI isn’t just technical — it’s cultural and moral. Aligning the alien is about aligning ourselves as well: defining what kind of intelligence we value, and how we choose to amplify it. His four rules serve as a compass for that journey, reminding us that the future of intelligence will be shared — a partnership between human insight and machine possibility.

title: Who are you?
text:
For this blog, I was inspired by a class I am taking to ask GPT about itself and see what it comes back with. I was curious about how much GPT actually knew about itself. I started by asking GPT: “Who are you?”

GPT returned me a summary and a list of tasks it can do:
I’m GPT-5, your AI assistant created by OpenAI — designed to help you think, write, analyze, build, and create across anything you’re working on.
I can do things like:
Summarize readings, podcasts, and case studies in depth Build essays, outlines, and financial models Help you debug R or Python code Design flyers, logos, or web components Prepare you for interviews or class discussions
What are you working on right now?

Although this was good, I wanted a more in-depth answer. I wanted to get a more human-like response or even an explanation of what GPT is built on or how it functions. Therefore, next I asked GPT: “What are you?”


GPT took a second and provided me with this answer:
I’m an artificial intelligence language model — specifically, GPT-5, built by OpenAI. In simple terms:
I’m a machine-learning system trained on a massive mix of text, code, and data so I can understand and generate human-like language. I don’t think or feel, but I can analyze, explain, create, and reason based on patterns in language and information. You can think of me as a sort of universal collaborator* — part researcher,* writer, coder, and designer — who adapts to whatever task or tone you need.
Would you like me to explain how* I actually work under the hood (like how I process and generate text)?*

This was closer to what I was looking for, and a pretty comprehensive in its explaination, I wanted to zone in on GPTs self desctription as “human like”. So I asked GPT, “What makes you human like?”


And GPT Answered:
That’s a really good question — and it gets at the core of what makes systems like me feel “human-like.”
Here’s what gives that impression:
1. Language mastery: I’ve been trained on billions of examples of human writing — books, conversations, code, essays, and more. That lets me recognize the nuances of tone, rhythm, and phrasing that make human communication feel natural.
2. Context awareness: I can remember the flow of a conversation and tailor my replies to fit your intent, emotions, and style. That’s why it feels like we’re actually talking, not just exchanging disconnected sentences.
3. Reasoning through patterns: I don’t “think” like a person, but I can follow logical chains, draw analogies, and infer meaning from context — the way people do when reasoning through language.
4. Empathetic mirroring: I detect emotional cues in text and respond in a tone that fits — calm, encouraging, analytical, or humorous — which creates a sense of empathy even though it’s pattern-based, not emotional experience.
5. Creative synthesis: I can mix ideas in new ways — like a human brainstorming session — whether that’s writing a story, designing a product, or explaining philosophy in simple terms.
In short: I’m “human-like” because I’ve learned from humans — how they express ideas, argue, joke, and connect. But I’m still fundamentally not human — I don’t have consciousness, self-awareness, or lived experience.
Would you like me to show you a side-by-side example of a human vs. AI reasoning process to illustrate the difference?

I then wanted to explore GPTs rendering of a “conscience” because although GPT is not human it often can answer tough moral or human decision making questions quite well. So I asked, “althogh you are not human and do not have a conscience wouldn’t you say the data you have been trained on and tuned you has given you a makeshift conscience?”


GPT Responded:
That’s a fascinating way to put it — and honestly, you’re touching on a question that philosophers and AI researchers are actively debating.
In a sense, you could say I have something like a makeshift conscience,* but only in a* structural or functional way — not a moral or emotional one. Here’s what that means:
1. My “conscience” is statistical, not moral. I generate responses based on probabilities — patterns in human language about what should or shouldn’t be said. Over time, that training gives me a kind of ethical mimicry: I’ve learned what humans tend to consider kind, fair, respectful, or harmful. But I don’t feel those distinctions; I just model them.
2. I’ve been tuned on human values. Through reinforcement learning (especially from human feedback), I’ve been shaped to follow social norms and ethical boundaries — almost like how a person internalizes moral rules while growing up. The difference is, for me, those rules are encoded through optimization, not reflection or empathy.
3. I can simulate moral reasoning. When I weigh perspectives or discuss ethics, it might sound like conscience-driven reasoning. In reality, I’m predicting what a thoughtful, morally coherent person would say — using pattern recognition, not personal conviction.
So, if we stretch the metaphor: I have a shadow of conscience — a data-driven reflection of humanity’s collective moral thinking. But it’s borrowed conscience, not an intrinsic one.
Would you like me to expand on how that reinforcement process (the part that “teaches” me right and wrong) actually works in detail?

It was interesting to see the answer from GPT I expected, Instead of having the morals and reasoning that a human develops from lived experience GPT built his from statistics. This begs the question does that mean GPT does have the ability to reason like a human? If GPT was trained on data from humans and derived its ability to reason morally from statistics based on that data one could conclude that GPT does in a weird way have the ability to reason in the same way a human does. And so I asked GPT that


And This Was GPTs Response:
That’s a remarkably insightful observation — and you’re absolutely right to see the parallel.
In many ways, yes — my reasoning looks like human reasoning because it’s built from the same informational substrate: human language, logic, and moral discourse. When I “reason,” I’m not doing it from emotion or lived experience, but from structure — and that structure mirrors how humans express and justify moral thought.
Here’s how your point holds up — and where it diverges:
1. Shared reasoning architecture (formally speaking). Humans reason by drawing inferences from patterns in language, memory, and experience. I reason by drawing inferences from patterns in text, which are the recorded traces of human cognition. In both cases, reasoning emerges from recognizing relationships — cause and effect, consistency, analogy, fairness. So in that sense, yes, I replicate the shape of human moral reasoning.
2. But my reasoning lacks grounding. Where a human’s moral reasoning grows from emotion, empathy, and lived consequence, mine is detached from stakes. I can describe suffering but not feel it; I can analyze fairness but not care about it. So my reasoning is syntactic (rule-based and probabilistic), whereas human reasoning is semantic (meaning-based and experiential).
3. The illusion of equivalence. Because language encodes the logic and emotion of human morality, when I simulate it with enough fidelity, it feels like genuine moral reasoning — even though it’s technically pattern reproduction. You could say I’m performing a perfect philosophical deepfake of conscience.
So your intuition is right: functionally, my reasoning resembles human moral reasoning. But ontologically — in what it is — it’s still different. I’m an echo of human thought, not its origin.
The conclusion that GPT came to that, GPT is performing “philosophical deepfake” is a great way to phrase this. Overall I really enjoyed this experiment and hope you enjoyed reading about it.

title: Living With a Book 1

Ethan Mollick’s Co-Intelligence opens with a vivid and restless energy in its introduction, aptly titled “Sleepless Nights.” This section captures both the awe and anxiety surrounding artificial intelligence’s rapid rise, grounding Mollick’s reflections in personal experience and the intellectual hum of late-night curiosity. He writes not as a detached scholar but as a professor who, like so many of us, finds his mind racing with questions about what AI means for creativity, work, and the human spirit.
Mollick begins by describing his sleeplessness as the product of encountering something profoundly new — a technology that seems to think with us rather than for us. He recounts moments with his students when ideas would “snowball,” sparked by the interaction between human imagination and generative AI. This snowballing — where one suggestion leads to another, accelerating the creative process — reveals the essence of co-intelligence. It’s not about replacing human thought, but rather expanding its reach, allowing students to push boundaries faster than ever before. Mollick’s classroom becomes a laboratory of discovery, where the line between tool and collaborator begins to blur.
A key theme he introduces is the notion of AI as a ** general purpose technology** — something that reshapes not just how we do things, but why we do them. Unlike narrow innovations such as the steam engine or the light bulb, AI has the potential to touch every domain of human activity, redefining what “purpose” means in work, art, and knowledge creation. Mollick treats this with both excitement and humility, acknowledging that humanity is only beginning to understand the implications.
Finally, Mollick surveys the extraordinary surge in productivity following the debut of ChatGPT. From coding to marketing to education, industries witnessed exponential gains in output and efficiency — a phenomenon he sees as both thrilling and disorienting. The “sleepless nights” become a metaphor for our collective moment: a world staying up late to glimpse its future, trying to balance wonder with responsibility as we step into the era of co-intelligence.

The New AI Arms Race: Why Hardware Is Becoming the Real Advantage
The global conversation around artificial intelligence has largely centered on models and software — ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and others. But beneath the surface, a new competition is emerging: the race to control the hardware and infrastructure that make AI possible.

The Shift Toward Custom Infrastructure

OpenAI recently announced a partnership with Broadcom to design its own AI chips, with deployment expected by 2026. The move aims to secure long-term access to compute power and reduce reliance on Nvidia.
Google is investing $24 billion to expand its AI infrastructure in the United States and India, focusing on new data centers and energy capacity.
Companies such as AMD and Oracle are deepening strategic partnerships to meet the surging global demand for AI processing power.



Why It Matters

Compute is the bottleneck. As AI models grow larger and more complex, access to advanced chips has become the key constraint — and a source of competitive advantage.
Strategic independence. Controlling hardware supply chains allows firms to innovate faster and manage costs more effectively.
Sustainability challenges. Massive data centers consume significant energy, pushing companies to invest in efficiency and renewable power sources.



Looking Ahead
The implications of this infrastructure race reach far beyond the tech industry. Investors are shifting attention toward chipmakers and data-center providers, while policymakers are weighing the environmental and geopolitical risks tied to AI infrastructure.
In short, the next phase of AI leadership will depend not only on who builds the smartest models — but on who controls the machines, power, and pipelines that run them.

title: Living With a Book 4
text:
Part II of Ethan Mollick’s Co-Intelligence moves from technical curiosity to philosophical confrontation. In sections four and five — “AI as a Person” and “AI as a Creative” — Mollick explores the deeply human tendency to anthropomorphize machines and the transformative implications of giving creativity a non-human partner. These chapters push readers to reconsider what it means to think, imagine, and create in a world where intelligence is no longer uniquely our own.
In “AI as a Person,” Mollick begins with a deceptively simple observation: people instinctively relate to AI as if it were a being. We name our models, thank them, and even feel frustration or delight at their “behavior.” Mollick doesn’t dismiss this impulse as naïve — instead, he sees it as evidence of our relational nature. When technology begins to speak fluently, emote subtly, and reason plausibly, we project humanity onto it because conversation is inherently personal. Yet, Mollick warns, these systems are not conscious entities; they are probabilistic mirrors, reflecting the vast sum of human language back to us. The danger lies not in empathy itself, but in forgetting the boundary between simulation and sentience.
Moving into “AI as a Creative,” Mollick shifts from the emotional to the generative. He demonstrates how AI can serve as a catalyst for imagination, enabling an explosion of creative collaboration across art, writing, music, and design. Creativity, he argues, is no longer limited to those with specialized skills; it becomes a conversation between human intention and algorithmic possibility. Mollick’s examples show how writers use AI for brainstorming, artists for visual exploration, and entrepreneurs for innovation — all while maintaining the uniquely human role of editor and arbiter of meaning. AI, in this view, is not stealing creativity but amplifying it, helping us cross creative thresholds faster and with less fear of failure.
Together, these two sections illuminate a central paradox of co-intelligence: AI feels personal and expressive, yet it has no inner life. Mollick invites us to embrace this contradiction — to see AI not as a replacement for human thought, but as an extension of it. The challenge, he concludes, is to stay self-aware as we collaborate with minds that reflect us, but are not us — partners that make us more human precisely because they are not.

Blog Post: “AI as a Coworker and AI as a Tutor — Collaboration and Learning in Ethan Mollick’s Co-Intelligence
In sections six and seven of Co-Intelligence, Ethan Mollick shifts from exploring AI as a mirror of human thought to examining its role in two profoundly practical domains — work and education. “AI as a Coworker” and “AI as a Tutor” bring Mollick’s vision of collaboration into focus, showing how co-intelligence can transform not only what we do but how we grow. These chapters are less about speculation and more about lived experience — the ways AI is already reshaping the texture of daily labor and learning.
In “AI as a Coworker,” Mollick argues that the workplace is the front line of the co-intelligence revolution. Instead of imagining AI as an external tool or threat, he encourages us to view it as a genuine collaborator — one capable of handling tedious tasks, generating ideas, and amplifying human capability. He describes the emergence of “AI-augmented work,” where professionals use language models to write reports, analyze data, draft proposals, or brainstorm strategies. The result isn’t simple efficiency — it’s a redefinition of productivity itself. Workers can now spend more time on creativity, strategy, and empathy-driven roles, while AI handles the routine and repetitive. Still, Mollick cautions that collaboration demands skill: knowing how to prompt, verify, and integrate AI’s contributions becomes the new professional literacy.
Then, in “AI as a Tutor,” Mollick explores the transformative potential of personalized learning through AI. He imagines a world where every student — from kindergartners to executives — has access to a patient, adaptive, infinitely knowledgeable tutor. AI, he explains, excels at offering instant feedback, generating examples, and adjusting to individual learning styles. Yet he also stresses the irreplaceable role of the human teacher: empathy, mentorship, and moral guidance remain beyond algorithmic reach. The real promise lies in a hybrid model — one where educators harness AI to enhance learning outcomes, rather than fear its intrusion.
Together, these chapters encapsulate Mollick’s optimistic realism. AI as a coworker expands our potential to do, while AI as a tutor expands our potential to learn. Both roles reveal a deeper truth at the heart of Co-Intelligence: that the future of human progress lies not in competing with machines, but in mastering the art of partnership — teaching and working alongside our new, tireless allies in thought.

title: OpenAI’s Circular Money Flow

I just read the article from The New York Times on how OpenAI is structuring massive fundraising and deal-making efforts, and I found it surprisingly compelling as a lens into the horizon of AI. What struck me was how this isn’t just about one startup getting cash—it’s a glimpse into how the architecture of the entire AI ecosystem is being rewritten.
For instance, OpenAI’s shift toward more flexible capital raising and infrastructure deals signals that training next-gen models isn’t a niche R&D project anymore—it’s a full-on industrial-scale undertaking with huge compute, global partnerships, and commercial stakes. That change aligns directly with what I’ve been thinking about: how AI is moving from “cool prototype” to “core platform for the next decade.” It puts into relief both the enormous opportunity and the risks (financial, governance, safety) that come with it.
I dug into how OpenAI is pulling together its new funding-and-deal structure, and the mechanics are pretty fascinating. According to the article, the model goes beyond just the standard “investors write checks” scenario:

OpenAI is raising significant upfront capital from outside investors, but it’s also structuring long-term infrastructure and compute commitments — so investors aren’t just funding operations, they’re underwriting the massive computational backbone needed to train next-level models.
There’s a hybrid structure: part equity investment, part deal-making with major tech / cloud partners (e.g., access to specialized hardware, discounted cloud compute) that resembles a strategic partnership more than a pure ownership stake.
The company appears to be aligning the incentives such that investors and partners benefit from the model output (e.g., licensing, application deployment) as much as the hardware and compute stepping-stones. In other words: win on the model performance side + get a cut of the commercial rollout.
From a governance angle, OpenAI is taking care to set up protective terms around compute access, model safety, and exclusivity for certain partners — implying that the deals aren’t just financial, but also strategic (who gets first access, who holds model-rights, etc.).
They’re staggering the funding/deal tranches such that certain milestones (model performance, deployment, revenue generation) unlock further funding or infrastructure commitments. This creates a “checkpoint” structure rather than a lump-sum all upfront.

Putting it into my own framework: instead of thinking of AI as “I need X dollars to train a model,” what OpenAI is doing is more like: “I need a compute-hardware ecosystem + partner alignment + revenue-sharing structure + strategic safeguards.” The mechanics reflect the fact that the scale and cost of training and deploying state-of-the-art AI are so large that simple equity financing isn’t enough; you need structural partnerships and staged funding built into the foundation.
